section_1.title: Prerequisite Intuition: The Pulse and the Sine Wave
section_1.content: Briefly revisit the Fourier Transform foundation: Any signal can be decomposed into sine waves. Introduce the extreme ends: a single 'spike' (Dirac delta) in time requires infinite frequencies to construct, while a single perfect sine wave exists for infinite time.
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'snap' (short burst of sound) versus a 'pure hum' (tuning fork tone).

section_2.title: Defining the Trade-off: Time-Frequency Reciprocity
section_2.content: Introduce the Uncertainty Principle in signals: $\Delta t \cdot \Delta f \geq C$. Explain that narrowing the window in the time domain necessarily widens the spread in the frequency domain. Use animation to show the 'squeezing' of a Gaussian pulse.
section_2.example: Animation of a 'rubber band' pulse: compressing it horizontally in the time-axis causes it to 'pop' and expand vertically in the frequency spectrum.

section_3.title: Visualizing the Gaussian Optimal
section_3.content: Highlight why the Gaussian function is the 'Goldilocks' signal—it is the only function that achieves the minimum possible uncertainty bound. Show a side-by-side graphical comparison of a rectangular window vs. a Gaussian window.
section_3.example: A character 'Dr. Fourier' demonstrating how the Gaussian shape minimizes 'spill-over' (sidelobes) in both time and frequency.

section_4.title: Application: Radar and Chirp Signals
section_4.content: Apply the principle to real-world technology. Explain the dilemma: short pulses provide high resolution for distance (time) but lose precision in identifying velocity (frequency). Introduce the 'Chirp' signal as a clever workaround.
section_4.example: A bat using 'chirps': explaining how the frequency sweep allows the bat to determine both exact distance and relative speed of a moth despite the uncertainty limit.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Summary
section_5.content: Synthesize the core takeaway: You cannot perfectly localize a signal in both domains. This isn't a failure of our tools, but a fundamental property of wave mathematics.
section_5.example: A final graphic showing a 'See-Saw' balancing act: as Time Precision goes up, Frequency Precision must go down.
